blocks.x: Why capital planning needs to change
The cost of getting capital decisions wrong has gone up, which makes capital planning for property managers worth doing from data rather than instinct.

Borrowing can cost more since the Bank of Canada [raised its policy rate to 2.50%](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/10/fad-press-release-2026-10-28/) on October 28, 2026, and building costs more too: [Altus Group's 2026 Cost Guide insights](https://www.altusgroup.com/insights/caution-in-2026-optimistic-for-2027-cost-guide-insights/) say costs in Winnipeg rose by 4% or more in 2025.

Electricity costs are rising too. [Manitoba Hydro's electricity revenue increases](https://www.pubmanitoba.ca/v1/contact-us/media/pubs/2026-nr/nr-mh-gra-fiscal-2026-2028-march-19-2026-english.pdf) of an average 3.5% in 2027 and 3.0% in 2028 follow a 4.0% general rate increase in 2026. Your customer class may pay more or less than the average.

Meanwhile, rents are flattening. Winnipeg's average unfurnished one-bedroom asking rent has fallen three months in a row, [liv.rent's October 2026 report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) shows. Owners cannot count on rent growth to cover inefficient spending.
The capital planning data property managers already have
Most property managers sit on more useful data than they realize:

What it reveals
rows: Recurring problems by unit, system or building area
Comfort issues such as drafts, noise and cold units
Which units turn most often and why
Which units lease slowly or need concessions

blocks.x: The challenge is pulling it together. A simple spreadsheet, building by building, is often enough to start.
Our view: let repeat problems drive the plan

The most useful signal in most buildings is repetition. A window that gets a work order every winter, a door that needs adjusting every month, a unit that turns every year: these are the places where capital spending can save money.
A data-driven approach typically follows four steps:
**Collect** two to three years of work orders, complaints and turnover data.
**Group** issues by location and type (windows, doors, floors, masonry).
**Cost** the repeat repairs and compare them with the cost of replacement.
**Rank** projects by payback, risk and tenant impact.
For example, add up what a building spends in a year adjusting and repairing failing entry doors, then compare that with a written replacement quote to see how quickly new doors would pay back.
To sort the ranked list into what to do now and what can wait, use the [three budget buckets](/blog/bank-of-canada-rate-hike-renovation-budgets): protect the asset, earn revenue and nice to have.
Windows, doors and flooring are where data pays off

Many capital projects are installation work: windows, doors, flooring. These are often the items with the clearest data trail, because failures generate work orders and complaints. [Commercial renovation work](/services/commercial-renovations) can turn that data into targeted fixes:
**Windows:** replacing units with failed seals or frames can reduce condensation and comfort complaints.
**Doors:** replacing worn entry, suite and service doors can cut repair calls and improve security. Suite doors are often part of the fire separation, so check requirements first.
**Flooring:** durable flooring can reduce turnover and replacement costs.
Presenting the plan to owners
A data-backed capital plan can be easier to approve. Owners will want to see:
What the problem is costing now.
What the fix will cost.
When it will pay back, in reduced repairs, energy savings or better retention.
What happens if the work is deferred.
Pairing that analysis with written contractor quotes gives owners more confidence to commit.
Common pitfalls
Data-driven planning works best when the data is reliable. Watch for a few common problems.

Work orders that are closed without notes make it hard to see patterns. Complaints recorded only by phone or in emails are easy to miss. Utility data that is not normalized for weather can be misleading. And capital plans that ignore tenant feedback may target the wrong problems.
Simple fixes help: standard categories for work orders, a single place to log complaints and regular reviews of the data.
A sample ranking

This is a made-up example, not a real building or job. Imagine a 40-unit building where the data shows 25 window-related work orders a year, 30 door repairs and a high turnover rate in ground-floor units. Ranking by cost and impact might put ground-floor windows and the main entrance door first, because they generate the most complaints and repair calls.

Suite doors might come second, replaced at turnover. Hallway flooring, with fewer complaints but high visibility, might be third. The data does not make every decision, but it makes the trade-offs clear.
The bottom line

When capital is expensive, guesswork is costly. Property managers who use the data they already have can target spending at the problems that cost the most, and present plans that owners can approve with confidence.
